Website · Guides · Showcases Quick start · How REA works · What you can analyze · Showcases · Build RL environments · FAQ · Documentation npx rea-agents setup Important Get REA from morluto/rea , rea.tools , or the rea-agents npm package . Follow the installation and release links from these official sources. A similar repository name or copied README does not establish that a download is official. See a feature in an app that you want in your own product? Ask your agent to investigate it with REA. It can inspect the app without its source code, explain how the feature works, show the evidence, and build a version for your project. REA connects your agent to tools for inspecting native binaries, JavaScript and Electron apps, .NET assemblies, and websites. You can also use the same tools from your terminal. Analysis runs locally, and results include the evidence and limitations behind each conclusion. Setup registers REA with your agent and installs matching workflow instructions. Native analysis can use an existing Hopper, Ghidra, IDA or Kuna installation; setup can optionally install Hopper with approval. Static JavaScript analysis needs no native analysis engine. Visit the REA website for setup instructions, illustrated guides, and real case studies. On Linux, Ghidra, JADX, firmware tool launches and static JavaScript/Electron analysis require a procps-compatible ps on REA's PATH for process ownership checks. Recovery steps are in docs/installation.md under "Linux owned-process prerequisite". With Node.js and npm installed, run: npx rea-agents setup Choose your agents, review the proposed changes, and approve them. Setup adds REA's MCP server and matching workflow instructions, with backups of existing configuration. Restart your agent afterward. Setup records the selected runtime and REA entry script directly. If acquired through a package runner, keep its cache entry available. Run package acquisition from a trusted directory outside the target project. Installation and recovery details are in the setup guide below. Setup supports Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Grok Build and other agents . See installation and setup for provider configuration and manual MCP registration and Claude Code/Codex plugin installation. MCP uses compact input schemas by default to reduce context overhead. Set REA_MCP_INPUT_SCHEMA_PROFILE=full in your MCP registration when you need the complete advertised field guidance and nested validation details. Both profiles keep the full tool set and canonical server validation. See "Compact input schema profile" in the MCP contracts guide. Complete output schemas are advertised by default. If your client caps the complete tools/list frame, set REA_MCP_OUTPUT_SCHEMA_PROFILE=compact to bound each advertised output schema, or off to omit output schemas entirely. Both settings keep canonical server-side validation and complete structured results. See "Output schemas" in the MCP contracts guide. Understand how search works in the Notes app, show me the evidence, and build a similar feature for my project. Replace Notes with your target app and the feature you want to understand. Inspect an extracted JavaScript/Electron app directory or ASAR: npx -y rea-agents@latest analyze-javascript-application /absolute/path/to/app --json The result includes modules, imports, Electron boundaries and their evidence. Replace the path with your target, such as "D:/apps/example" on Windows. To install the rea command for regular use: npm install --global rea-agents rea --help For native analysis, configure a provider first. See the CLI and Evidence guide for native commands, provider selection, snapshots and scripting. REA changes quickly, and new releases include frequent bug fixes. Keep your installation up to date. For a CLI installed with npm install --global or bun add --global : rea update rea --update is an alias for this verified workflow and accepts the same global output flags. Use rea update when combining it with other command controls. Updater commands retain at most 4 MiB of stdout and stderr combined. Oversized metadata replies are rejected after the command exits; verbose installs continue with bounded diagnostics. Human progress output respects terminal backpressure and waits for submitted writes to finish. Bun global updates require Bun 1.2.17 or later. With an older Bun release, upgrade Bun manually before running rea update . To refresh your agent registrations and skill, run the setup command printed by the update. If you use npx , update your agent setup with: npx rea-agents@latest setup Review the setup changes and restart your agent. For one-off CLI commands, use npx rea-agents@latest followed by the command. With Bun, use bunx rea-agents@latest in place of npx rea-agents@latest . Your agent calls REA through MCP to inspect the target and trace relevant code. REA returns findings with their evidence. The agent uses them to ask follow-up questions, explain the behavior, or write and test an implementation. CLI commands use the same workflows. Open the full-size figure . REA requires Node.js 22.x (>=22.23.4), 24.x (>=24.22.1), or 26.12.1+, plus npm. Additional tools and host support depend on the target: Static JavaScript and .NET inspection read the supplied files without running the application. Runtime capture runs or interacts with the selected target using your user permissions; each runtime guide describes its effects. For offline native-binary inspection, REA also supports caller-supplied GNU objdump and Rizin. See the reverse-engineering tools guide for provider setup, CLI commands, and Evidence limitations. REA does not install or update either provider. Native formats and host support vary by provider. See Hopper and Ghidra setup , the IDA guide (including an optional native MCP bridge), the Kuna decompiler guide , and experimental Windows Ghidra support . Ghidra also supports 16-bit DOS analysis . For large binaries, raise the provider's startup deadline with REA_GHIDRA_STARTUP_TIMEOUT_MS or REA_HOPPER_STARTUP_TIMEOUT_MS . For provider selection, see the CLI guide . Check release availability for features added since the latest npm release. DX-Ball: reconstruct a sound-pan calculation Follow a sound call into its position-to-pan helper, inspect the instructions, and turn incomplete pseudocode into C. The reconstruction passes 3,205 original-x86 cases and reproduces all 63 compiled function bytes. Read the case study Inspect the original PC-98 game's 16-bit instructions, recover the fixed and aimed angle calculations, and compare the reconstructed C++ with the historical compiler output. Run it with AgentEnv, then add tasks and reward checks for RL training or evaluation. Read the guide · Watch the video If you've used REA on something interesting, we'd love to see it. Share your case in an issue or a pull request , including the target, your question, how REA helped, and what you found. Give an AI agent a local environment to practice tasks such as finding an issue or creating a folder, without running the original app. Use it for reinforcement learning (RL) or to test how well an agent completes tasks. REA turns recorded API requests and responses into tools the agent can call. The environment uses the recorded data and supports changes only when the recording confirms their effects. With REA set up in your agent, replace the example URL and folder tasks below with your own: Use REA to build an RL environment from my test web app at http://127.0.0.1:3000. Cover listing, creating, renaming, and deleting folders. You may create and remove test folders. Leave existing data unchanged. Save it in a folder named my-env. Check which operations work and tell me how to run it. Use the command line instead Use these commands if you already have a file containing the app’s recorded browser requests and responses. Running the result also requires AgentEnv and Docker. rea environment-build ./session.har ./my-env --name my-env --json agent-env run ./my-env REA exports a runnable environment with a basic test to check that it starts and responds. Use it with your RL framework to define task goals, add reward checks, and run training. Build an environment · Environment reference · Watch the demo on X Any agent that supports local MCP servers. Setup configures the supported agents ; other clients can use manual MCP registration . Deep native analysis uses Hopper, Ghidra, IDA or Kuna, depending on the target and operation. Static JavaScript and .NET inspection work without a native analysis engine. Setup can install Hopper after approval; Ghidra, IDA and Kuna use your existing installations. See provider setup for the options and their supported targets. REA starts Hopper when an operation needs it. On macOS, a first-run dialog may ask you to choose demo mode or activate your license. Complete that prompt in the same user session before your first CLI/MCP operation or unattended job. Open Hopper manually if needed. See Hopper startup and troubleshooting . The skill supplies investigation instructions for your agent. Use npx rea-agents setup to register REA's MCP server and install the matching instructions, then restart your agent. See skill-only installation . Native analysis returns pseudocode and assembly. JavaScript/Electron analysis recovers modules and their relationships. Your agent uses these findings to write and test an implementation; the showcases give worked examples. REA analyzes targets locally. Your agent receives the tool results, and its model provider has its own data policy. Update first; a recent release may already fix it. For a CLI installed with npm install --global or bun add --global : rea update For agent setup through npx : npx rea-agents@latest setup If you're using an agent, complete the setup refresh and restart it. Retry the same task. If the problem persists, open an issue with your REA version, target type, steps to reproduce and error output. Start with the website's worked guides .
